chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Abdullah ibn Ishaq al-Alawi, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Hilal, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I enter the market of the Muslims, meaning this people who claim Islam, and I buy the furs from them for trade. So I say to its owner: 'Is it not purified (slaughtered)?' He says: 'Yes.' So is it correct for me to sell it upon the condition that it is purified?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'No. But there is no problem if you sell it and say: 'The one from whom I bought it stipulated to me that it is purified.''

I said: 'And what spoils that?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The permitting by the people of Iraq of the dead (animal), and they claim that tanning the skin of the dead is its slaughter. Then they are not pleased to lie about that except against the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family).'

key_terms.لِلْمَيْتَةِ: The dead animal (one not ritually slaughtered)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling tanned fur from non-slaughtered animals in Islamic trade?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) addresses the specific fiqh of *takhayyur* (discretion in speech) to avoid *ghish* (deception) when selling tanned hides, ruling that one should not assert the hide is 'purified' (*zakiyyah*) as an inherent fact if it is from a *maytah* (dead animal), since the people of Iraq equate tanning with slaughter. Instead, he permits stating that the previous owner stipulated it was purified, thereby shifting the claim to a contractual condition rather than a biological reality. This ruling highlights the Shia emphasis on precise linguistic truthfulness in commercial transactions, distinguishing between the legal status of tanning and the ontological status of the animal's death.
